title: Why is a piggy bank a pig? (It was the clay, not the animal)
description: The pig in piggy bank is an accident of language. Centuries ago, the cheap clay used for household pots was called 'pygg' — and the little money pots made from it slowly turned into the animal we know.

body.heading: It started with a word for clay
paragraphs: In medieval England, metal was expensive, so ordinary households kept dishes and pots made from a cheap orange clay called pygg. Loose coins went into a pygg pot or jar on the shelf — the household's savings, quite literally kept in clay.

By the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, the clay's name and the farm animal's name sounded identical, and potters — who never miss a joke — began making the money pots pig-shaped. The pun outlived the clay: the pots became ceramic, then plastic, then apps, and the pig stayed.

body.heading: The pot you had to break
paragraphs: The oldest piggy banks had no hole in the bottom. To spend your savings you had to smash the pot — a design that made saving the default and spending an event. Every coin dropped in was a small decision, and the pot's growing weight was the only balance enquiry available.

There is a lesson in that friction. Modern saving works best the same way: money that is slightly inconvenient to reach gets spent less than money one tap away. The pig understood behavioural economics centuries early.

body.heading: Keep the pig, keep the point
paragraphs: A piggy bank still earns its shelf space today — for children learning that coins become something bigger, and for adults who find a visible, physical savings habit sticks when an invisible account balance does not.
Choose a goal, name the pig if you must, and let it fill. Some technologies survive because the idea inside them was never really about the technology.

takeaway: Piggy banks are pigs because of a clay called 'pygg' and a potter's pun — and their break-to-open friction is still a saving lesson worth keeping.
